bib.title: From LLMs to LLM-based Agents for Software Engineering: A Survey of Current, Challenges and Future

read.skipped: Reference list read only up to entry [57] (about chars 0-275,000 read in full); the remaining references (about 30,000 chars) were not read in full.

question: How do LLM-based agents differ from plain LLMs across six software-engineering topics, in tasks, benchmarks and evaluation metrics?
contributions: A first survey, to the authors' knowledge, that separates LLM and LLM-based-agent work in software engineering across six topics (requirements, code generation, autonomous learning and decision making, design, test generation, security and maintenance).
A working six-criterion definition of an LLM-based agent for SE (Table V).
A comparison of tasks, benchmarks and evaluation metrics used by LLM papers versus agent papers, and of the 82 models used in experiments.
A list of challenges and future directions for LLM-based agents in SE.

results.claim: The survey states that no accepted definition of an LLM-based agent exists for software engineering, and offers its own.
results.setup: Section III-E, software engineering scope; criteria synthesised from works from the first half of 2024 (SWE-agent, CodeAgent, AutoCodeRover, GOEX) with MetaGPT, AgentVerse, Reflexion, ExpeL as support.
results.quote: Currently, there is no comprehensive and widely accepted definition specifying the exact capabilities an LLM must exhibit to be considered an LLM-based agent

results.claim: Six criteria define an agent; an architecture counts if it meets most of them, with 1 to 4 fundamental and 5 and 6 advanced.
results.setup: Table V; applied by the authors by judgement to the surveyed frameworks, not validated.
results.quote: we define an LLM architecture as an agent if it meets most of the criteria listed in Table V
results.note: Criteria 1-4: LLM as brain, decision-making and planning, autonomous tool choice, selecting the best of multiple homogeneous results. 5-6: multi-turn context, autonomous learning and adaptability.
results.where: Section III-E, p. 8, Table V p. 9

results.claim: Criteria 5 and 6 are not strictly necessary for agent status.
results.setup: Section III-E definition.
results.quote: beneficial but not strictly necessary for an LLM to be initially classified as an agent

results.claim: The survey classes Self-collaboration (multiple GPT-3.5-turbo role agents) as an agent although it lacks tools.
results.setup: Section V-B; self-collaboration framework [101] on HumanEval and MBPP.
results.quote: Although it lacks external tool integration and dynamic adjustment capabilities
results.note: The Cycle framework [96], by contrast, is classed as an advanced LLM application because its execution follows a fixed pattern (Section V-A).

results.claim: The survey collected 139 papers on LLMs and LLM-based agents in SE.
results.setup: DBLP and arXiv, keyword AND/OR queries (Table IV), snowballing, manual screening; excludes papers under 7 pages and grey literature; window latter half of 2023 to before December 2024.
results.quote: Overall, we identified 139 relevant papers.
results.note: Section X-A also says 'we summarized a total of 110 papers'. Fig 12 topic counts sum to 153 because papers can sit in several topics; Fig 1 axis values sum to about 138.

results.claim: The collection window is the latter half of 2023 to before December 2024.
results.setup: Section II-A.
results.quote: Since the collection primarily focuses on the latter half of 2023
results.note: The arXiv stamp is v2, 13 Apr 2025; v1 was August 2024.

results.claim: 82 unique LLMs were used across the 139 papers; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA2 and Codex are the most frequent.
results.setup: Section X-A, includes comparison models.
results.quote: we identified a total of 82 unique large language models

results.claim: Agent papers cluster on autonomous learning and decision making (nearly 30%), while LLM papers cluster on requirements and security.
results.setup: Fig 12: 77 agent paper instances; Autonomous 23 (29.9%), Code 20 (26.0%), Security 13 (16.9%), Design 9, REQ 6, Test 6. LLM: 76 instances, REQ 20 (26.3%), Security 17 (22.4%), Code 16.
results.quote: comprising nearly 30% of all agent-related papers

results.claim: Most frequent metric for agent papers is Success Rate; for LLM papers it is Accuracy.
results.setup: Fig 14 top-10 metrics; LLM side Accuracy 20.9%, Pass Rate 16.4%, F1 11.9%, Correctness 11.9%, Exact Match 6.0%. Agent side Success Rate 20.0%, Accuracy 15.7%, Pass@1 12.9%.
results.quote: metric used by agents is Success
results.note: Text says 'Success Rate (20.0%), followed by Pass@1 (12.9%), Accuracy (15.7%)', which is not in rank order. Win Rate is printed 4.5% in text; Fig 14 shows other values.

results.claim: Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were used in the requirements-engineering agent studies; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 appear in 16 and 12 of 23 autonomous-topic agent papers.
results.setup: Autonomous Learning and Decision Making agent papers, Section X-A.
results.quote: 12 out of 23 papers and 16 out of 23 papers, respectively

results.claim: Using LLMs for test generation alone is cheaper and enough; a full agent framework for it is 'overkill'.
results.setup: Section VIII-C, analysis, no cost measurement given.
results.quote: Considering the cost, using LLMs for test generation only is enough and more cost saving than using LLM-based agents.
results.note: Section VII-C adds: 'In terms of efficiency and cost, LLMs are still slightly superior to LLM-based agents in text generation and vulnerability detection.'

results.claim: Reflexion lifted HumanEval first-pass success from 80.1% to 91.0%.
results.setup: Python programming; ALFWorld success +22%, HotPotQA +14% in the same paragraph.
results.quote: first-pass success rate on the HumanEval Python programming task increased from 80.1% to 91.0%

results.setup: Pass@1 on SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix; dated, since later agents far exceed this.

limits: The agent criteria are the authors' synthesis, applied by judgement and not validated against any benchmark; the survey itself says there is no consensus on the autonomy, planning and tool use needed to count as an agent (Section X-D, challenge 1).
The survey runs no experiments; every performance number is quoted from the surveyed papers, with differing models, budgets and benchmarks, and no leakage control.
Scope is software engineering only; agent claims are not shown to transfer to other domains.
Paper counts are inconsistent: 139 in text, 110 in Section X-A, 153 summed in Fig 12.
Authors concede open problems: no standard evaluation, multi-agent error propagation, tool-integration fragility, little cross-task transfer, scarce simulation data, opaque reasoning (Section X-D).
Background statements are weak: GPT-4 'approximately 175 billion' parameters, PaLM 'up to 54 billion', OPT as comparable in size to GPT-4; do not cite.
Typos: 'fixed 3982 out of 2780 defects' for FixAgent on Codeflaws; MGSM described as 'Multimodal Generalized Sequence Modeling'.
Results are 2024-era (SWE-bench 12.5%, GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and have dated.
practices: Treat tool use, planning and evaluation of candidate outputs as the basic level of agency; add multi-turn context and autonomous learning as advanced traits (Section III-E).
Do not build a full agent framework for plain test generation; an LLM alone is cheaper and enough (Section VIII-C).
Use fresh or leakage-controlled benchmarks (EvalGPTFix, PRIMEVUL, ConDefects, EvalPlus) because older benchmarks overstate performance (Sections IX-A, X-C).
Give agents explicit memory pools, experience tracking and self-evaluation for complex debugging and requirements work (Section X-E, item 2).
